analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal child labor for anyone under 18 to have direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved: it was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, children can legally work on farms at younger ages than in other industries, and tobacco farms are treated like any other farm even though handling the plant can expose workers to nicotine absorption through the skin. This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to say that any job where a worker under 18 touches tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves is "oppressive child labor," which is generally illegal. It closes the agricultural exception for tobacco specifically, without touching minors' ability to do other farm work. The bill was introduced in June 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors who work or would work in tobacco farming, most of them in states like North Carolina, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Virginia. Tobacco harvest work is done by hand, and workers routinely handle the plants for hours; research on the crop has documented nicotine absorption through the skin, nausea, and vomiting among teen workers. The bill would give the Labor Department clear authority to treat that contact as illegal child labor. Farmworker advocates and the families of teen workers also benefit from a clearer legal line.

how_it_helps.text: It changes the legal definition of 'oppressive child labor' under the Fair Labor Standards Act so that any job giving a worker under 18 direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves counts as illegal oppressive child labor.
It removes tobacco-related agriculture from the existing carve-outs that let children work in agriculture, closing the loophole that currently permits minors to handle the crop.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco growers and farm labor contractors, who lose access to under-18 workers during a labor-intensive, hand-harvested crop season. Tobacco leaf processors and cigarette manufacturers could face modest upstream compliance and labor-cost effects. Consumers would see little direct effect.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise labor costs for tobacco growers, who rely on seasonal hand labor, and the record contains no phase-in, exception, or assistance for small farms adjusting to the new rule.

The bill is narrow: it covers only direct contact with tobacco plants and dried leaves, so minors could still legally work in other hazardous agricultural jobs and in tobacco operations that do not involve touching the crop.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: keeping children out of direct contact with a crop whose harvested form is toxic, at little cost to consumers. The honest cost is borne by tobacco growers, for whom under-18 workers have been a real part of the harvest labor pool, and the bill does not offer those growers an alternative labor arrangement or phase-in. An objection a good-faith skeptic would raise is that the bill is narrow — it covers only tobacco and only direct contact, leaving older teens free to work in other hazardous farm jobs and leaving tobacco farms otherwise unregulated. But on its own terms the bill does what it says, and it died without anyone having to weigh those trade-offs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or brought it up; it sat there until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on June 12, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
Twenty-five House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The action history shows no activity after the referral: no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee.

The bill's mechanism was to amend Section 3(l) of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, adding tobacco contact to the definition of oppressive child labor and explicitly removing tobacco agriculture from the child-labor carve-outs that otherwise apply to farm work.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers and the wider tobacco supply chain are better off, because they keep access to under-18 labor for harvesting and handling the crop. Children working on tobacco farms remain unprotected by any federal statute specifically naming tobacco work.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco growers who use under-18 labor

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban under-18 workers from direct contact with tobacco.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action on it for the remaining eighteen months of the Congress.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the committee that controlled the bill's fate was chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Tobacco growers and farm labor contractors
industries.note: The bill would bar the under-18 workers who make up part of the tobacco harvest workforce, raising labor costs for growers who rely on seasonal hand labor. The crop's toxicity is precisely why the labor is cheap and why the bill targets it.

Leaf handled by children flows into the supply chain sold to processors and cigarette makers; the bill would push child contact out of the chain and add compliance pressure upstream. That burden is the point of the bill, not a side effect.
